title: AI-Voyager: A Public-Interest System for Human-AI Civic Reasoning to Contest and Shape the Rules That Govern AI

Title:AI-Voyager: A Public-Interest System for Human-AI Civic Reasoning to Contest and Shape the Rules That Govern AI
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Governments are writing rules for artificial intelligence that decide what counts as an automated decision or a harm, often before the people they affect have a chance to question them. We introduce AI-Voyager, a public-interest system for human-AI civic reasoning, in which people and AI work together to understand, contest and shape the rules that govern AI. A resident can find their city's rules on AI in hiring or upload their country's AI strategy, read it as an affected worker would, open the passage behind any answer, and draft a revision. Its architecture turns 3,653 governance documents from city, state, federal and national governments into passages that keep their page and edition, and retrieves evidence through bounded agentic search that verifies each statement. On 360 new questions that require finding the relevant documents, it reached 83.0% macro recall, against 80.5% for the strongest baseline, 73.7% without iterative search and 99.1% on a benchmark with fixed documents. In a study with 24 participants new to two AI bills, most proposed changes asked how provisions would apply. Participants chose lenses for the kind of explanation they wanted, and citations signaled grounding but rarely led them to check the source. By binding AI assistance to the exact text of public documents, this work introduces a grammar of operations and a design space that inform how such systems are designed and evaluated, and how people take part in governing AI.

report.summary: AI-Voyager is a public-interest, citation-grounded system that helps residents read, contest and revise government AI rules with AI assistance.
report.background: Governments are rushing to write rules for artificial intelligence, deciding what counts as an automated decision or a harm, often before affected people can meaningfully question them. Those rules are scattered across city, state, federal and national documents, written in legal and technical language that is hard for ordinary residents to parse. At the same time, retrieval-augmented AI systems are making it easier to search large document collections, but they can obscure provenance or produce unsupported claims. AI-Voyager responds to both problems by turning 3,653 governance documents into page- and edition-preserving passages, then using bounded agentic search to verify statements. The project sits at the intersection of civic technology, AI governance and human-AI collaboration, asking how public participation can be built into the rules that govern AI rather than added after the fact.
key_points: AI-Voyager lets a resident find local rules on AI in hiring or upload a national AI strategy, then read the document from the perspective of an affected worker. Users can open the passage behind any answer and draft a revision, turning passive reading into contestation and proposal-making.

The system converts 3,653 governance documents into passages that retain their page and edition. It retrieves evidence through bounded agentic search that verifies each statement, a design choice meant to keep AI assistance tied to the exact text of public documents rather than free-floating summaries.

On 360 new questions requiring users to find relevant documents, AI-Voyager reached 83.0% macro recall, compared with 80.5% for the strongest baseline and 73.7% without iterative search. On a benchmark with fixed documents, it reached 99.1%, showing that open-ended retrieval remains the harder problem.

In a study with 24 participants new to two AI bills, most proposed changes asked how provisions would apply. Participants chose lenses for the kind of explanation they wanted, and citations signaled grounding but rarely led them to check the original source.

The paper contributes a grammar of operations and a design space for human-AI civic reasoning. By binding assistance to public text and evaluating both retrieval and user behavior, it offers a model for how civic AI systems can be designed and assessed.
report.impact: For the AI industry, AI-Voyager pushes policy question-answering toward provenance-first retrieval, bounded agents and evaluation that separates fixed-document accuracy from open-ended search. That distinction matters for developers building legal, regulatory or compliance tools: strong benchmark scores can hide weak document-finding performance. The user study also exposes a design gap—citations may signal trustworthiness without prompting verification—so interfaces need stronger nudges toward source checking. For regular users, the system could lower the barrier to participating in AI rulemaking, letting workers, advocates and residents examine and revise the rules that affect them. But it also shows that access alone is not participation; the real impact depends on whether civic groups, governments and developers adopt such systems transparently and fund public-interest maintenance.
report.tools: Watch for AI-Voyager's code and data release via the arXiv paper. To replicate or extend it, explore open governance corpora such as GovInfo, LegiScan and city council portals; retrieval frameworks like LlamaIndex, Haystack or LangChain; and RAG evaluation tools such as RAGAS. Add passage-level provenance and citation-verification layers, and pair them with public comment or legislative-tracking platforms for civic use.
